transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Head of ML - Stonegate), Priya Sharma (Infra Lead), Daniel Brooks (CISO)

Summary: Discovery focused on Dedicated capacity: reserved GPUs, isolation needs, burst strategy, autoscaling expectations, security/compliance requirements. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, leaning Dedicated with VPC and burst to hosted. Wants benchmarks and pricing before committing.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - I'm Maya, AE for Redwood, and Ethan our solutions engineer. Liam, Priya, Daniel, thanks for making time. quick agenda: understand your workload, latency & throughput targets, isolation/compliance constraints, and what success looks like.

[00:22] Liam: Hi, yeah thanks. quick context - we run several user-facing LLM features: chat summarization, doc search reranking, and some high-volume embedding generation for analytics. right now it's all on prem with a mix of GPUs and a managed API for some prototypes. We're evaluating Redwood for predictable throughput and easier ops.

[01:10] Ethan: got it. what are the rough qps and latency SLOs per workload? and do you need single-tenant isolation or just network-level separation?

[01:28] Priya: For chat summarization, p95 latency budget is 350-400ms, target p50 around 120ms. Embeddings are large batch jobs overnight but occasional spikes during reporting hours - those need burst handling. In terms of isolation, we need dedicated tenancy for the model hosts; can't mix other customers' workloads on the same GPUs. network isolation via VPC is also required.

[02:05] Maya: that makes sense. so Dedicated capacity maps well — reserved GPU pools with VPC and tenant isolation. question: are you open to a hybrid where baseline traffic runs on Dedicated and spikes can burst to Hosted (with egress/data controls), or must everything remain on private infra?

[02:30] Liam: Ideally everything stays in our VPC, but we could consider controlled burst to Redwood Hosted if the data path is acceptable and logs/audit are preserved. Daniel will push on this, of course.

[02:44] Daniel: yeah security is the blocker. we need SOC 2, encryption at rest & in transit, KMS integration, and audit logs for requests. Also SSO and fine-grained RBAC for access. If burst to hosted means data leaves our control, that might be a no.

[03:05] Ethan: totally. we have options. Redwood Private gives a private control plane and everything in your VPC/on-prem. Dedicated supports VPC peering and can be provisioned in a customer-dedicated pool with disk encryption and KMS. For burst scenarios we can configure policy-based burst to Redwood Hosted but with stanza that redacts or routes certain data — there are tradeoffs.

[03:45] Priya: how does the reserved GPU sizing work? number of GPUs vs throughput? and what's the latency profile as load increases?

[04:00] Ethan: good q. we provision by GPU count and GPU type (A100, H100, or lower mem amps). throughput depends on model size, sequence length, and batching. for example with a 32k-ish LLM on an H100 you might achieve x tokens/sec; smaller models get more concurrency. we typically size by peak qps and target SLOs and then set an autoscale/burst policy.

[04:28] Liam: is there continuous batching? we need low latency for chat so batching can't add too much tail latency.

[04:38] Ethan: yes, the runtime does workload-aware batching and prefix/KV cache; for chat we keep KV cache hot on the reserved nodes to avoid cold-start penalties. batching is adaptive to preserve p95 latency. you can also carve out latency-priority lanes for conversational traffic.

[05:10] Maya: on the procurement side — committed capacity is monthly/annual. we can do a reserve with burst credits. pricing tiers depend on GPU SKU and committed hours. we'll share a draft pricing sheet as a next step.

[05:30] Daniel: about logs and audit — do you keep request-level logs on Redwood side? we require immutable audit trails for three years for some parts of the application.

[05:45] Ethan: by default we retain logs per your retention policy; for Dedicated we can ship logs to your SIEM via Kinesis or direct S3 in your account. Private gives the most control. we can also integrate with your KMS to prevent Redwood from accessing plaintext keys.

[06:12] Priya: what's the typical burst strategy customers use? and how quickly can you scale up additional GPUs?

[06:25] Maya: many customers keep a baseline reserved pool sized for steady-state, plus a small buffer of burst capacity that can warm up quickly. we can pre-warm instances or use thin warm standby nodes. scale-up times vary — for additional Dedicated GPUs in the same region it's usually minutes to tens of minutes depending on infra, but if we need to fallback to Hosted it's near-instant.

[06:52] Liam: minutes to tens of minutes is okay but for flash spikes we need sub-10s to avoid user-visible errors. is there a strategy for graceful degradation?

[07:05] Ethan: yes. you can configure policy-level fallbacks: (1) serve a lighter model variant on the reserved pool, (2) route non-sensitive traffic to Hosted fallback, or (3) queue with a short retry/backoff and send status to clients. customers often combine 1 & 2: keep a smaller low-cost, lower-latency model on reserved nodes and burst non-sensitive requests to Hosted.

[07:35] Daniel: hmm that could work if we classify data sensitivity. For finance data, we can't send PII to hosted endpoints. Does Redwood support routing rules by data classes?

[07:47] Ethan: yes, we can route by tag, header, or route. Redwood's smart routing supports policies that match on request metadata and choose model/cluster. for Dedicated we can have an allowlist that prevents certain routes from ever leaving your VPC.

[08:05] Priya: about autoscaling config, do you do vertical scaling or just add nodes? and how do you control cold starts?

[08:18] Ethan: we scale horizontally by adding GPU nodes. to avoid cold starts we use KV cache warmers and prefix caching; you can also reserve a tiny pool of warm standby nodes to handle cold-start sensitive workloads. we expose metrics so you can tune thresholds.

[08:45] Liam: ok, can you walk through a sample architecture for Dedicated in our VPC? what gets installed, what stays in Redwood control plane, and what logs are visible?

[09:00] Ethan: high level: we deploy model-serving nodes in a subnet in your VPC (customer-owned or dedicated account depending on the offering). the control plane can be customer-managed (Private) or Redwood-managed with VPC peering. model artifacts and checkpoints reside in your storage (optional) or in an encrypted store accessible via your KMS. audit logs and metrics are pushed to your S3/CloudWatch. the control plane manages scheduling, routing, and can be configured for canary rollouts.

[09:45] Daniel: are there existing customers in finance with similar controls? reference customers help our auditors.

[09:55] Maya: yes, we have banks and fintechs using Dedicated and Private — happy to share redacted references and compliance packs. we'll include SOC 2 and architecture diagrams in the follow-up.

[10:10] Priya: what's the onboarding timeline? from contract to traffic?

[10:20] Maya: typically 2-6 weeks: contract & security review (~1-2w), infra provisioning and networking (~1-2w), pilot/benchmarks (1w), then ramp. Private can add more time for on-prem.

[10:38] Liam: for the benchmark, we want to run our 7-step prompt set, and measure p50/p95 latency, token cost, and tail quiescence. can Ethan lead that?

[10:50] Ethan: absolutely. I'll put together a benchmark plan and the telemetry we collect. we'll want a representative traffic trace from you.

[11:05] Daniel: circling back to encryption keys — we need HSM-backed KMS and key rotation policy. Can Redwood support customer-managed keys?

[11:18] Ethan: yes, Dedicated and Private support customer-managed KMS/HSM. Redwood doesn't keep plaintext keys. we'll include details in the security document.

[11:35] Maya: any budget or procurement timeline we should know about?

[11:42] Liam: Q2 procurement window, decision by end of April ideally. Budget is allocated but final sign-off pending benchmarks and security ok.

[11:55] Priya: what about GPU SKUs — we want a cost/perf comparison for A100 vs H100 for our mix of models.

[12:05] Ethan: we'll include comparative numbers and recommendations — often for smaller models A100 is fine, for large context H100 yields better perf per watt but costs more. quantization/profiles also change the equation.

[12:28] Maya: any competitors you're talking to?

[12:32] Liam: we're looking at OpenAI's hosted, Anthropic for model options, and some cloud-managed offerings on AWS. pricing and security are key differentiators.

[12:45] Ethan: understood. we'll try to benchmark apples-to-apples and include cost comparisons.

[13:00] Maya: quick recap and next steps - we'll send pricing + SOC2 docs; Ethan will draft the benchmark plan and schedule a 2-hour run; Liam to share traffic traces and priors; Daniel to forward compliance questionnaire.

[13:22] Daniel: noted. also please include a short doc on 'what leaves Stonegate' for burst cases — we need clarity for legal.

[13:34] Maya: will do. any final Qs?

[13:40] Priya: one more — what's the SLA for Dedicated?

[13:45] Maya: Dedicated comes with SLA options depending on contract tier; typical uptime SLAs are 99.9% with latency targets defined per model/route. we'll include the SLA language in the SOW.

[14:00] Liam: great, thanks all. looking forward to the benchmark.

[14:05] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up by EOD tomorrow with the docs.

[14:12] (meeting ends)

Notes about transcript quality: automated transcription present; occasional mis-hears (e.g., 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cash', 'H100' as 'H one hundred'), some speaker overlap at the end of questions.
